blogTitle: NELAP/TNI Accreditation for Environmental Labs: A LIMS Readiness Guide
elevenlabsPodcastSourceText:
This bulletin was written by Confident LIMS and is being read to you using AI voice generation.

Environmental labs rarely lose accreditation because the chemistry was wrong. They lose it because nobody could find the record that proved the chemistry was right.

Here is the short version. NELAP, the National Environmental Laboratory Accreditation Program, is run by accreditation bodies, usually state agencies. They assess your lab against a standard written by The NELAC Institute, known as T-N-I. So no lab is T-N-I certified. Labs hold NELAP accreditation, assessed against T-N-I requirements.

Which version is in force? The twenty-sixteen T-N-I Environmental Laboratory Sector Standard. That is still the assessed version as of October twenty twenty-six. During twenty twenty-six, T-N-I posted draft revisions for comment, including volume one module two, on quality management system requirements. Drafts in a comment period are not requirements. If someone tells you there is a twenty twenty-four T-N-I standard you must comply with, ask them to point at the adoption notice.

Underneath nearly every requirement sits one question. Can you produce the evidence, tied to the sample, on demand?

Six things your lab information management system should be carrying. One, chain of custody captured as it happens, not reconstructed afterwards. Two, S-O-P and method version control, so a result from March points at the March S-O-P. Three, analyst competency and demonstration of capability, flagged before authorizations expire. Four, calibration and maintenance records that stay attached to the results produced on that instrument. Five, proficiency testing and fields of proficiency testing traceability, including corrective actions that actually closed. Six, an audit trail an assessor can follow without a chaperone.

Most labs run accreditation as a six-week sprint before the assessment. The alternative is boring in the best way. Evidence accumulates as work happens, so assessment week becomes a retrieval exercise instead of a reconstruction project.

One caution on language. Software does not make your lab accredited. Your accreditation body does that. A system helps you comply with recordkeeping and data integrity expectations. The work is still yours.

You can read the full guide on the Confident LIMS blog at confident lims dot com. Thanks for listening.
